note: Europa Strata profiles for smaller polities and peoples that the historical-basemaps borders name but the main era packs don't profile. Matched by basemap name; `when` limits an entry to tab:year stops. Sources per entry; general reference: Encyclopaedia Britannica.

profiles.name: Cyprus
profiles.summary: A Byzantine province until the rebel Isaac Komnenos seized it in 1184. Richard I of England took the island in 1191 on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it; from 1192 the French Lusignan dynasty ruled a crusader Kingdom of Cyprus until Venice took over in 1489.
profiles.description: A Byzantine province until the rebel Isaac Komnenos seized it in 1184. Richard I of England took the island in 1191 on his way to the Third Crusade and sold it; from 1192 the French Lusignan dynasty ruled a crusader Kingdom of Cyprus until Venice took over in 1489.
profiles.conflicts: Arab raids in earlier centuries; Richard I’s conquest (1191); Genoese seizure of Famagusta (1373); Mamluk invasion and the king’s capture (1426).
profiles.leaders: Isaac Komnenos; Guy of Lusignan and Amalric, the first Lusignan rulers; Peter I, who led the sack of Alexandria in 1365.
profiles.religion: Greek Orthodox majority under a Latin Catholic church hierarchy imposed by the Lusignan kings.
profiles.culture: A Greek-speaking island ruled by a French-speaking court, with Italian merchant colonies in Famagusta.
profiles.story: Lusignan Cyprus outlived the fall of Acre in 1291 and became the last Latin kingdom of the crusader East.
sources: P. W. Edbury, The Kingdom of Cyprus and the Crusades, 1191–1374 (1991)

profiles.name: Sardinia (the Judicates)
profiles.summary: After Byzantine control faded, Sardinia split into four self-governing realms called judicates (Cagliari, Arborea, Torres, Gallura), each ruled by a iudex. Pisa and Genoa competed for influence. Aragon claimed the island from 1297 and Arborea, the last judicate, gave in by 1420.
profiles.description: After Byzantine control faded, Sardinia split into four self-governing realms called judicates (Cagliari, Arborea, Torres, Gallura), each ruled by a iudex. Pisa and Genoa competed for influence. Aragon claimed the island from 1297 and Arborea, the last judicate, gave in by 1420.
profiles.conflicts: Pisan–Genoese rivalry over the island; Aragon’s conquest from 1323; long Arborean resistance.
profiles.leaders: Judges of Arborea, especially Eleanor of Arborea (d. c. 1404).
profiles.religion: Latin Christian, with Benedictine and other monasteries brought in from the mainland.
profiles.culture: Sardinian-language charters (condaghes) and the Carta de Logu law code of Arborea.
profiles.story: Eleanor of Arborea’s Carta de Logu stayed in force on the island until 1827.

profiles.name: Corsica
profiles.summary: Corsica was split among local lords under Pisan church overlordship until Genoa defeated Pisa at Meloria in 1284. Genoa then ruled the island, sometimes through the Bank of Saint George, until it was sold to France in 1768.
profiles.description: Corsica was split among local lords under Pisan church overlordship until Genoa defeated Pisa at Meloria in 1284. Genoa then ruled the island, sometimes through the Bank of Saint George, until it was sold to France in 1768.
profiles.conflicts: Pisa–Genoa wars; Aragonese claims; revolts by local lords against Genoa.
profiles.leaders: Archbishops of Pisa held church authority; later Genoese governors and the Bank of Saint George.
profiles.religion: Latin Christian, with Pisan Romanesque churches across the island.
profiles.culture: Mountain clan society with a Tuscan-influenced Corsican language.
profiles.story: The Pisan Romanesque churches built across the island in the 1100s still stand.

profiles.name: Kingdom of Georgia
profiles.summary: Bagrat III united the Georgian lands as one kingdom in 1008. David IV the Builder drove out the Seljuks, winning at Didgori in 1121 and taking Tbilisi in 1122, and the kingdom reached its height under Queen Tamar (1184–1213). Mongol rule from the 1230s and Timur’s invasions wore it down, and by the 1490s it had split into rival kingdoms and principalities.

David IV the Builder drove out the Seljuks, winning at Didgori in 1121 and taking Tbilisi in 1122, and the kingdom reached its height under Queen Tamar (1184–1213). Mongol rule from the 1230s and Timur’s invasions wore it down, and by the 1490s it had split into rival kingdoms and principalities.
profiles.conflicts: Seljuk wars; Didgori (1121); Khwarezmian and Mongol invasions (1220s–1240s); Timur’s campaigns (1386–1403).
profiles.leaders: Bagrat III; David IV the Builder; Queen Tamar; George V the Brilliant, who restored the kingdom after the Mongols.
profiles.religion: Georgian Orthodox Christianity, with monasteries such as Gelati at the centre of learning.
profiles.culture: A golden age of Georgian literature and church building.
profiles.story: Shota Rustaveli’s epic The Knight in the Panther’s Skin dates from Tamar’s reign.
sources: R. G. Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1994)

profiles.name: Armenia
profiles.yearsActive: Bagratid kingdom 885–1045; then Byzantine, Seljuk and Georgian overlords
profiles.summary: Around 1000 the Bagratid kings ruled from Ani, a city of churches on the Silk Road. Byzantium annexed Ani in 1045 and the Seljuks sacked it in 1064. In the 1100s and 1200s Armenian lords such as the Zakarids governed much of the region under Georgian protection.
profiles.description: Around 1000 the Bagratid kings ruled from Ani, a city of churches on the Silk Road. Byzantium annexed Ani in 1045 and the Seljuks sacked it in 1064. In the 1100s and 1200s Armenian lords such as the Zakarids governed much of the region under Georgian protection.
profiles.conflicts: Byzantine annexation (1045); Seljuk conquest after Manzikert (1071); Mongol invasions from the 1230s.
profiles.leaders: Gagik I of Ani; the Zakarid brothers Zakare and Ivane.
profiles.religion: Armenian Apostolic Church, with monastic centres such as Haghpat and Sanahin.
profiles.culture: Armenian stone churches, carved khachkar cross-stones and manuscript illumination.
profiles.story: Ani became known as the ‘city of 1001 churches’.
sources: R. G. Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times, vol. 1 (1997)

profiles.name: Buyid (Buwayhid) emirates
profiles.summary: The Buyids were a Shi‘i dynasty from Daylam that took Baghdad in 945 and ruled Iraq and western Iran in the caliph’s name. The Seljuk Turks ended their rule between 1055 and 1062. The basemap uses the label loosely for the upper Mesopotamian borderlands, where Kurdish and Arab dynasties also ruled.

The Seljuk Turks ended their rule between 1055 and 1062. The basemap uses the label loosely for the upper Mesopotamian borderlands, where Kurdish and Arab dynasties also ruled.
profiles.conflicts: Rivalry with the Hamdanids, Byzantium and the Ghaznavids; Seljuk conquest of Baghdad (1055).
profiles.leaders: Adud al-Dawla (d. 983), the strongest Buyid ruler.
profiles.religion: Twelver Shi‘i rulers who governed under the Sunni Abbasid caliph.
profiles.culture: Persian court culture in Arabic and Persian; patronage of scholars and hospitals in Baghdad.
profiles.story: Adud al-Dawla’s hospital in Baghdad was founded in the 980s.

profiles.name: Principality of Benevento
profiles.summary: Benevento was the longest-lived Lombard state in southern Italy. It survived Charlemagne’s conquest of the Lombard kingdom in 774 as an independent principality. By 1000 it had lost Salerno and Capua as separate states. In the 1000s the city passed to the papacy and the Normans took over its lands.

By 1000 it had lost Salerno and Capua as separate states. In the 1000s the city passed to the papacy and the Normans took over its lands.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with Byzantium, Arab raiders and Carolingian kings; Norman expansion in the 1000s.
profiles.leaders: Arechis II, who took the title of prince in 774.
profiles.religion: Latin Christian, with the abbeys of Monte Cassino and San Vincenzo al Volturno nearby.
profiles.culture: Lombard law and Beneventan script, a distinctive southern Italian handwriting.
profiles.story: The Beneventan script used by its monks gives the region its name in manuscript studies.

profiles.name: County of Aragon
profiles.summary: Aragon began as a small Pyrenean county around Jaca. In 1000 it was tied to the Kingdom of Pamplona (Navarre). After Sancho III of Navarre died in 1035, his son Ramiro I ruled Aragon on his own, and it later grew into the Crown of Aragon.

profiles.conflicts: Frontier warfare with the Muslim taifas of the Ebro valley.
profiles.leaders: Sancho III of Navarre; Ramiro I, the first king of Aragon (from 1035).
profiles.religion: Latin Christian, with mountain monasteries such as San Juan de la Peña.
profiles.culture: A Pyrenean frontier society that spoke an early form of Aragonese.
profiles.story: From this small county came the Crown of Aragon, later a Mediterranean power.

profiles.name: Duchy of Brittany
profiles.summary: Brittany was a Breton-speaking duchy in the far west of France. It recognised the French king as overlord but governed itself. In the 1300s the War of the Breton Succession ended with the Montfort dukes in power. Anne of Brittany’s marriages to two French kings led to Brittany’s union with France in 1532.

In the 1300s the War of the Breton Succession ended with the Montfort dukes in power. Anne of Brittany’s marriages to two French kings led to Brittany’s union with France in 1532.
profiles.conflicts: Norman and Angevin pressure; War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364); French invasion (1487–1491).
profiles.leaders: Alan IV; John IV and John V of Montfort; Duchess Anne (1488–1514).
profiles.religion: Latin Christian, with strong cults of local saints.
profiles.culture: Breton language in the west and Gallo in the east, with a ducal court at Nantes.
profiles.story: Anne of Brittany married Charles VIII and then Louis XII of France.

profiles.name: Sámi lands (Sápmi)
profiles.summary: The Sámi are the indigenous people of northern Scandinavia, Finland and the Kola Peninsula. They had no state of their own and lived in local communities called siida, based on hunting, fishing and, later, reindeer herding. Norwegian, Swedish and Russian rulers competed to tax them from the Middle Ages on.

They had no state of their own and lived in local communities called siida, based on hunting, fishing and, later, reindeer herding. Norwegian, Swedish and Russian rulers competed to tax them from the Middle Ages on.
profiles.conflicts: Overlapping tax claims by Norway, Sweden and Novgorod (later Russia).
profiles.leaders: No kings; leadership came from siida elders and noaidi (shamans).
profiles.religion: Traditional Sámi religion, with Christian missions growing from the 1600s.
profiles.culture: Sámi languages, joik song and a herding and fishing economy.
profiles.story: Norse and Russian sources describe the Sámi as fur traders and skiers.
sources: N. Kent, The Sámi Peoples of the North (2014)

profiles.name: Northern forest peoples
profiles.summary: The basemap uses this label for the forest and tundra peoples of the far northeast. They include Finno-Ugric and Samoyedic groups who lived by hunting, fishing and the fur trade. They had no state. Novgorod traders, and later Moscow, gradually brought them into a tribute system.

They include Finno-Ugric and Samoyedic groups who lived by hunting, fishing and the fur trade. They had no state. Novgorod traders, and later Moscow, gradually brought them into a tribute system.
profiles.conflicts: Tribute collection by Novgorod and later Moscow, especially for furs.
profiles.leaders: No state rulers; kin and clan leaders.
profiles.culture: Hunting, reindeer herding and the fur trade.
profiles.story: Novgorod’s ‘Yugra’ fur expeditions reached the Urals in the 1000s and 1100s.

profiles.name: Karelians
profiles.summary: The Karelians are a Finnic people of the lands between the Gulf of Finland, Lake Ladoga and the White Sea. Around 1000 they traded furs with Novgorod. Sweden and Novgorod later fought over Karelia and divided it in the Treaty of Nöteborg (1323).
profiles.description: The Karelians are a Finnic people of the lands between the Gulf of Finland, Lake Ladoga and the White Sea. Around 1000 they traded furs with Novgorod. Sweden and Novgorod later fought over Karelia and divided it in the Treaty of Nöteborg (1323).
profiles.conflicts: Swedish–Novgorodian wars over Karelia.
profiles.religion: Pagan religion, gradually replaced by Orthodox Christianity under Novgorod’s influence.
profiles.culture: Karelian oral poetry, later collected in the Kalevala.
profiles.story: Birch-bark letters found in Novgorod include a short text in a Finnic language.

profiles.name: Finns (Suomi)
profiles.summary: This label covers the Finns of southwest Finland around 1000. They lived in farming and trading communities with no central state. Swedish crusades and Catholic missions brought the region under Sweden from the 1100s and 1200s.
profiles.description: This label covers the Finns of southwest Finland around 1000. They lived in farming and trading communities with no central state. Swedish crusades and Catholic missions brought the region under Sweden from the 1100s and 1200s.
profiles.conflicts: Swedish crusades into Finland; Novgorodian raids.
profiles.religion: Pagan religion, followed by Catholic conversion under Sweden.
profiles.culture: Iron Age farming and hill forts.
profiles.story: ‘Suomi’ is still the Finnish name for Finland.

profiles.name: Chuds
profiles.summary: ‘Chud’ is the old Russian name for the Finnic peoples east of the Baltic, especially the ancestors of the Estonians and Votes. The Russian Primary Chronicle lists them among the peoples who invited the Varangians to rule.
profiles.description: ‘Chud’ is the old Russian name for the Finnic peoples east of the Baltic, especially the ancestors of the Estonians and Votes. The Russian Primary Chronicle lists them among the peoples who invited the Varangians to rule.
profiles.conflicts: Raids and campaigns by Kiev and Novgorod; later the Livonian crusade.
profiles.story: The battle on the ice of Lake Peipus (1242) was fought on Lake Chud, as Russians call it.

profiles.name: Curonians (Kurs)
profiles.summary: The Curonians were a Baltic people of the coast of modern Latvia and Lithuania, known as seafarers and raiders. German crusaders conquered them in the 1200s, and Courland is named after them.
profiles.description: The Curonians were a Baltic people of the coast of modern Latvia and Lithuania, known as seafarers and raiders. German crusaders conquered them in the 1200s, and Courland is named after them.
profiles.conflicts: Raids on Scandinavia; the Livonian crusade.
profiles.culture: Seafaring, hill forts and amber trade.
profiles.story: Danish and Swedish chronicles describe Curonian raids across the Baltic.

profiles.name: Kimek–Kipchak confederation
profiles.summary: The Kimek–Kipchak confederation was a union of Turkic tribes on the Irtysh and the steppe east of the Volga. By the early 1000s the Kipchak tribes had pushed west and taken over the Pontic steppe, where Rus called them Polovtsy and Byzantines called them Cumans.
profiles.description: The Kimek–Kipchak confederation was a union of Turkic tribes on the Irtysh and the steppe east of the Volga. By the early 1000s the Kipchak tribes had pushed west and taken over the Pontic steppe, where Rus called them Polovtsy and Byzantines called them Cumans.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with the Oghuz and Pechenegs; later raids on Rus.
profiles.religion: Tengrist religion, with some Islamic and Manichaean influence.
profiles.story: The Kipchak language became the basis of the later Golden Horde’s Turkic.

profiles.name: Volga Bulgaria
profiles.summary: Volga Bulgaria was a Turkic state at the meeting point of the Volga and Kama. It adopted Islam in 922, when ibn Fadlan arrived as the caliph’s envoy. It grew rich on the fur trade from its capital Bolghar, until the Mongols destroyed it in 1236.
profiles.description: Volga Bulgaria was a Turkic state at the meeting point of the Volga and Kama. It adopted Islam in 922, when ibn Fadlan arrived as the caliph’s envoy. It grew rich on the fur trade from its capital Bolghar, until the Mongols destroyed it in 1236.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with the Rus principalities; Mongol conquest (1236).
profiles.leaders: Almış, the ruler who received the caliph’s mission.
profiles.culture: Trade in furs, slaves and silver between the northern forests and the Islamic world.
profiles.story: Ibn Fadlan’s report on his journey also describes the Rus traders he met.

profiles.name: Arran
profiles.summary: Arran is the medieval name for the land between the Kura and Araxes rivers, now in Azerbaijan. Around 1000–1100 the Kurdish Shaddadid dynasty ruled much of it from Ganja, until the Seljuks took control.
profiles.description: Arran is the medieval name for the land between the Kura and Araxes rivers, now in Azerbaijan. Around 1000–1100 the Kurdish Shaddadid dynasty ruled much of it from Ganja, until the Seljuks took control.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with Georgia, Shirvan and the Seljuks.
profiles.religion: Islam, with Christian Albanian and Armenian communities.
profiles.story: The poet Nizami Ganjavi (d. c. 1209) was born in Ganja.
sources: V. Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953)

profiles.name: Shirvan (the Shirvanshahs)
profiles.summary: Shirvan was a principality on the Caspian coast of modern Azerbaijan, ruled by the Shirvanshahs from Shamakhi and later Baku. It survived for centuries as a client of larger powers until the Safavids annexed it in 1538.
profiles.description: Shirvan was a principality on the Caspian coast of modern Azerbaijan, ruled by the Shirvanshahs from Shamakhi and later Baku. It survived for centuries as a client of larger powers until the Safavids annexed it in 1538.
profiles.conflicts: Raids from the steppe; Georgian, Seljuk and Mongol overlordship; Safavid conquest (1538).
profiles.leaders: Shirvanshahs of the Yazidid and Kasranid dynasties.
profiles.story: The Palace of the Shirvanshahs in Baku dates from the 1400s.

profiles.name: Alania
profiles.summary: Alania was a Christian kingdom of the Alans, an Iranian-speaking people of the North Caucasus. It was allied with Byzantium and Georgia, and the Mongols destroyed it in 1238–1239. The Ossetians are their descendants.
profiles.description: Alania was a Christian kingdom of the Alans, an Iranian-speaking people of the North Caucasus. It was allied with Byzantium and Georgia, and the Mongols destroyed it in 1238–1239. The Ossetians are their descendants.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with the Khazars; Mongol invasion (1238–1239).
profiles.leaders: Alan kings who married into the Georgian royal family.
profiles.religion: Orthodox Christianity, adopted under Byzantine missions in the 900s.
profiles.story: Church ruins in the upper Kuban valley mark the old Alan capital.

profiles.name: Khazar Khaganate (remnant)
profiles.summary: The Khazars were a Turkic khaganate between the Volga, Don and Caucasus. They controlled steppe trade for three centuries, and their elite adopted Judaism. Sviatoslav of Kiev broke their power in 965–969, and by 1000 only a weak remnant was left.
profiles.description: The Khazars were a Turkic khaganate between the Volga, Don and Caucasus. They controlled steppe trade for three centuries, and their elite adopted Judaism. Sviatoslav of Kiev broke their power in 965–969, and by 1000 only a weak remnant was left.
profiles.conflicts: Arab–Khazar wars; Sviatoslav’s campaigns (965–969).
profiles.leaders: The khagan and the bek, who held the real power.
profiles.religion: A Jewish ruling elite, with Muslim, Christian and pagan subjects.
profiles.culture: A trading state that charged tolls on the Volga trade.
profiles.story: Their capital Atil, on the Volga delta, has never been firmly located.
sources: P. B. Golden et al. (eds.), The World of the Khazars (2007)

profiles.name: Serbian principalities
profiles.summary: Around 1000–1100 the Serbs were split between Raška in the interior and Duklja on the coast, mostly under Byzantine overlordship. Stefan Nemanja (r. 1166–1196) later united them and founded the Nemanjić state.
profiles.description: Around 1000–1100 the Serbs were split between Raška in the interior and Duklja on the coast, mostly under Byzantine overlordship. Stefan Nemanja (r. 1166–1196) later united them and founded the Nemanjić state.
profiles.conflicts: Revolts against Byzantium; wars with Hungary.
profiles.leaders: Vukan of Raška; Constantine Bodin of Duklja.
profiles.religion: Christianity, between Rome and Constantinople until the Serbian Orthodox Church became self-governing in 1219.
profiles.story: Duklja’s rulers received a royal crown from the pope in 1077.

profiles.name: Pechenegs
profiles.summary: The Pechenegs were Turkic nomads who held the Pontic steppe from the 800s. Byzantium paid them to fight its enemies, and they also fought Kiev. Byzantium and the Cumans crushed them at Levounion in 1091.
profiles.description: The Pechenegs were Turkic nomads who held the Pontic steppe from the 800s. Byzantium paid them to fight its enemies, and they also fought Kiev. Byzantium and the Cumans crushed them at Levounion in 1091.
profiles.conflicts: Siege of Kiev (968); raids into Byzantium; Levounion (1091).
profiles.religion: Tengrist religion, with some conversions to Islam and Christianity.
profiles.story: The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII described their eight tribes in the 900s.

profiles.name: Kingdom of Croatia
profiles.summary: Medieval Croatia became a kingdom under Tomislav around 925. After its native dynasty died out, the Croatian nobles accepted Coloman of Hungary as king in 1102. Croatia kept its own institutions inside the union.
profiles.description: Medieval Croatia became a kingdom under Tomislav around 925. After its native dynasty died out, the Croatian nobles accepted Coloman of Hungary as king in 1102. Croatia kept its own institutions inside the union.
profiles.conflicts: The succession war after 1091; Venetian rivalry on the Dalmatian coast.
profiles.leaders: Tomislav; Peter Krešimir IV; Demetrius Zvonimir; Coloman of Hungary.
profiles.religion: Catholic Christianity, with Glagolitic liturgy on the coast.
profiles.culture: A Dalmatian town and Slavic hinterland.
profiles.story: The Baška tablet (c. 1100) is one of the oldest Croatian inscriptions.

profiles.name: Bulgaria
profiles.yearsActive: First Empire to 1018; Byzantine 1018–1185; Second Empire 1185–1396
profiles.summary: In the Balkans the basemap uses this label for the Bulgarian lands. Byzantium conquered the First Bulgarian Empire in 1018. The Asen brothers founded the Second Bulgarian Empire in 1185, ruling from Tarnovo. The Ottomans conquered it between 1393 and 1396, so by 1400 the label is out of date.
profiles.description: In the Balkans the basemap uses this label for the Bulgarian lands. Byzantium conquered the First Bulgarian Empire in 1018. The Asen brothers founded the Second Bulgarian Empire in 1185, ruling from Tarnovo. The Ottomans conquered it between 1393 and 1396, so by 1400 the label is out of date.
profiles.conflicts: Basil II’s war (1014–1018); the Asen revolt (1185); Ottoman conquest (1393–1396).
profiles.leaders: Peter and Ivan Asen; Kaloyan; Ivan Asen II; Ivan Shishman.
profiles.culture: Old Church Slavonic literature and the Tarnovo school of writers.
profiles.story: Ivan Asen II’s Tarnovo was a centre of Slavic Orthodox learning.

profiles.name: Black Hats (Karakalpaks)
profiles.summary: ‘Karakalpak’ means ‘black hat’ in Turkic. Rus chronicles call the Turkic nomads who settled as border guards for Kiev the Chorni Klobuky, or ‘black hoods’. The basemap places the label schematically.
profiles.description: ‘Karakalpak’ means ‘black hat’ in Turkic. Rus chronicles call the Turkic nomads who settled as border guards for Kiev the Chorni Klobuky, or ‘black hoods’. The basemap places the label schematically.
profiles.conflicts: Border service for Kiev against the Cumans.
profiles.story: They are distinct from the modern Karakalpaks of Uzbekistan, who share the name.

profiles.name: Maskut
profiles.summary: A small principality on the Caspian coast north of Derbent, known from Arab and Armenian sources. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.
profiles.description: A small principality on the Caspian coast north of Derbent, known from Arab and Armenian sources. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.
profiles.conflicts: Wars among neighbouring Caucasian states; Seljuk invasions from the 1060s.
profiles.religion: Christian or Muslim, depending on the ruling house.
profiles.culture: Mountain and valley communities speaking Caucasian languages, Armenian, Georgian, Arabic or Persian.
profiles.story: These small states show how fragmented the Caucasus was before David IV’s Georgia and the Mongols.
sources: V. Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband (1958)

profiles.name: Emirate of Derbent
profiles.summary: An Arab-led emirate based at the fortress city of Derbent, the Caspian ‘gate’ between the steppe and the Middle East. The Hashimid dynasty ruled it until the Seljuk era. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.name: Sarir (Khunzakh)
profiles.summary: The Christian Avar kingdom of Sarir in highland Dagestan, centred on Khunzakh. It later converted to Islam. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.name: Kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget
profiles.summary: A Bagratid Armenian kingdom in the Lori region, founded in the 980s. In the 1100s it became a vassal of Georgia. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.name: Principality of Khachen (Artsakh)
profiles.summary: An Armenian princely state in the mountains of Artsakh (Karabakh). Local princes kept it going under Seljuk, Georgian and Mongol overlords. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.
profiles.description: An Armenian princely state in the mountains of Artsakh (Karabakh). Local princes kept it going under Seljuk, Georgian and Mongol overlords. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.religion: Christian or Muslim, depending on the ruling house.
profiles.culture: Mountain and valley communities speaking Caucasian languages, Armenian, Georgian, Arabic or Persian.
profiles.story: These small states show how fragmented the Caucasus was before David IV’s Georgia and the Mongols.
sources: V. Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband (1958)

profiles.name: Durdzuks
profiles.summary: The Georgian name for the Vainakh highlanders, ancestors of the Chechens and Ingush. They lived in clan communities with no state. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.name: Lakz
profiles.summary: A highland principality in southern Dagestan, linked to the Lezgins, mentioned by Arab geographers. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.summary: An eastern Georgian kingdom that David IV the Builder annexed into united Georgia in 1104. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.summary: An Arab-ruled city-state at Tbilisi that lasted from the 700s until David IV took the city in 1122 and made it Georgia’s capital. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.name: Goghtn
profiles.summary: A district on the Araxes near Nakhchivan, historically an Armenian province, under Seljuk and local rulers in this period. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.name: Kingdom of Syunik
profiles.summary: An Armenian kingdom in the southern highlands (also called Baghk). The Seljuks took its last fortresses in 1170. It was one of many small states in the Caucasus between Byzantium, Georgia and the Seljuks.

profiles.name: Other Rus principalities
profiles.summary: After 1132 Kievan Rus split into separate principalities ruled by branches of the Rurikid dynasty, including Chernigov, Smolensk, Polotsk and Turov-Pinsk. They shared the Orthodox faith and the Rurikid dynasty. Most fell under Mongol overlordship from 1237–1240.
profiles.description: After 1132 Kievan Rus split into separate principalities ruled by branches of the Rurikid dynasty, including Chernigov, Smolensk, Polotsk and Turov-Pinsk. They shared the Orthodox faith and the Rurikid dynasty. Most fell under Mongol overlordship from 1237–1240.
profiles.conflicts: Princely feuds over Kiev; Cuman raids; Mongol invasion (1237–1240).
profiles.religion: Orthodox Christianity under the metropolitan of Kiev.
profiles.culture: Old East Slavic chronicles and church building.
profiles.story: The Tale of Igor’s Campaign describes a Novgorod-Seversky prince’s raid of 1185.

profiles.name: County of Toulouse
profiles.summary: Toulouse was a large southern French county and a centre of Occitan court culture. Around 1200 the Cathar heresy spread under Count Raymond VI. The Albigensian Crusade from 1209 broke the county, and it passed to the French crown in 1271.
profiles.description: Toulouse was a large southern French county and a centre of Occitan court culture. Around 1200 the Cathar heresy spread under Count Raymond VI. The Albigensian Crusade from 1209 broke the county, and it passed to the French crown in 1271.
profiles.conflicts: Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229); Muret (1213); Treaty of Paris (1229).
profiles.story: Simon de Montfort was killed besieging Toulouse in 1218.

profiles.name: Grand Principality of Ryazan
profiles.summary: Ryazan was a Rus principality on the Oka. The Mongols sacked it first, in December 1237. It survived as a buffer between Moscow and the steppe until Moscow annexed it in 1521.
profiles.description: Ryazan was a Rus principality on the Oka. The Mongols sacked it first, in December 1237. It survived as a buffer between Moscow and the steppe until Moscow annexed it in 1521.
profiles.conflicts: Mongol sack (1237); rivalry with Moscow.
profiles.leaders: Oleg Ivanovich (r. 1350–1402), who manoeuvred between Moscow and the Horde.
profiles.culture: A frontier principality on the forest-steppe edge.
profiles.story: The tale of Evpaty Kolovrat tells of Ryazan’s resistance to Batu.

profiles.name: Mamluk Sultanate
profiles.summary: The Mamluk Sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria from Cairo. Its rulers were slave-soldiers who seized power in 1250. They stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260 and took the last crusader cities by 1291. The Ottomans conquered it in 1516–1517.
profiles.description: The Mamluk Sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria from Cairo. Its rulers were slave-soldiers who seized power in 1250. They stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260 and took the last crusader cities by 1291. The Ottomans conquered it in 1516–1517.
profiles.conflicts: Ain Jalut (1260); fall of Acre (1291); Timur’s invasion of Syria (1400–1401); Ottoman conquest (1516–1517).
profiles.religion: Sunni Islam; the sultans hosted a shadow Abbasid caliphate in Cairo.
profiles.story: Historians such as Ibn Khaldun and al-Maqrizi worked in Mamluk Cairo.

profiles.name: Empire of Trebizond
profiles.summary: The Empire of Trebizond was a Greek state on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, founded by Komnenos princes as the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople. It lived on trade and diplomatic marriages until Mehmed II took it in 1461.
profiles.description: The Empire of Trebizond was a Greek state on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, founded by Komnenos princes as the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople. It lived on trade and diplomatic marriages until Mehmed II took it in 1461.
profiles.conflicts: Seljuk and Turkmen pressure; Ottoman conquest (1461).
profiles.leaders: Alexios I; Alexios III; David, the last emperor.
profiles.culture: Byzantine court culture on a Silk Road port.
profiles.story: Trebizond outlasted Constantinople by eight years.

profiles.name: Seljuk Sultanate of Rum and successor beyliks
profiles.summary: The Seljuks of Rum ruled central Anatolia from Konya. After their defeat at Köse Dağ in 1243 they were vassals of the Mongol Ilkhanate, and the sultanate ended around 1308. On the 1400 map the label stands for the Turkish beyliks that followed, such as Karaman.
profiles.description: The Seljuks of Rum ruled central Anatolia from Konya. After their defeat at Köse Dağ in 1243 they were vassals of the Mongol Ilkhanate, and the sultanate ended around 1308. On the 1400 map the label stands for the Turkish beyliks that followed, such as Karaman.
profiles.conflicts: Manzikert (1071); Myriokephalon (1176); Köse Dağ (1243).
profiles.religion: Sunni Islam, with Sufi orders and Christian subjects.
profiles.culture: Persian court culture, caravanserais and Konya’s mosques.
profiles.story: Rumi, the Sufi poet, lived and taught in Seljuk Konya.

profiles.name: Ilkhanate
profiles.summary: The Ilkhanate was a Mongol state founded by Hülegü, who sacked Baghdad in 1258. It ruled Iran, Iraq and eastern Anatolia from Tabriz. Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295. The state broke up after Abu Sa‘id died in 1335.
profiles.description: The Ilkhanate was a Mongol state founded by Hülegü, who sacked Baghdad in 1258. It ruled Iran, Iraq and eastern Anatolia from Tabriz. Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295. The state broke up after Abu Sa‘id died in 1335.
profiles.conflicts: Sack of Baghdad (1258); wars with the Mamluks and the Golden Horde.
profiles.religion: Shamanist and Buddhist rulers at first, then Islam from 1295.
profiles.story: Rashid al-Din’s world history was written for the Ilkhans.

profiles.name: Beylik of Aydın
profiles.summary: Aydın was a Turkish emirate on the Aegean coast around Smyrna and Ephesus (Ayasoluk), known for its fleets. The Ottomans annexed it, finally in 1426.
profiles.description: Aydın was a Turkish emirate on the Aegean coast around Smyrna and Ephesus (Ayasoluk), known for its fleets. The Ottomans annexed it, finally in 1426.
profiles.conflicts: Naval raids in the Aegean; the crusade that took Smyrna (1344).
profiles.story: The İsa Bey Mosque at Selçuk was built in 1375.

profiles.name: Principality of Moldavia
profiles.summary: Moldavia was founded around 1359 east of the Carpathians when Bogdan I broke away from Hungary. Under Alexander the Good (1400–1432) it controlled trade between the Black Sea and Poland.
profiles.description: Moldavia was founded around 1359 east of the Carpathians when Bogdan I broke away from Hungary. Under Alexander the Good (1400–1432) it controlled trade between the Black Sea and Poland.
profiles.conflicts: Pressure from Hungary and Poland; later Ottoman wars.
profiles.leaders: Bogdan I; Alexander the Good; later Stephen the Great.
profiles.culture: Romanian-speaking boyar society, with Church Slavonic as the written language.
profiles.story: Alexander the Good strengthened the port of Cetatea Albă (Akkerman).

profiles.name: Timurid Empire
profiles.summary: Timur conquered an empire from Central Asia to Anatolia and ruled from Samarkand. He defeated the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402. His successors ruled a smaller state from Herat and Samarkand until about 1507.
profiles.description: Timur conquered an empire from Central Asia to Anatolia and ruled from Samarkand. He defeated the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402. His successors ruled a smaller state from Herat and Samarkand until about 1507.
profiles.conflicts: Ankara (1402); sacks of Delhi, Baghdad and Damascus.
profiles.story: Ulugh Beg’s observatory at Samarkand was built in the 1420s.

profiles.name: Kingdom of Bosnia
profiles.summary: Tvrtko I made Bosnia a kingdom in 1377. Its silver mines made it rich. The Ottomans conquered it in 1463.
profiles.description: Tvrtko I made Bosnia a kingdom in 1377. Its silver mines made it rich. The Ottomans conquered it in 1463.
profiles.conflicts: Hungarian intervention; Ottoman conquest (1463).
profiles.leaders: Tvrtko I; Stephen Tomašević, the last king.
profiles.religion: Catholic, Orthodox and the independent Bosnian Church.
profiles.story: Thousands of stećci still stand across Bosnia.

names: Emirate of the White Sheep Turks
profiles.name: Aq Qoyunlu (White Sheep Turkmen)
profiles.summary: The Aq Qoyunlu was a Turkmen confederation that ruled eastern Anatolia, Iraq and Iran from Diyarbakır and later Tabriz. Ismail I’s Safavids replaced it in the early 1500s.
profiles.description: The Aq Qoyunlu was a Turkmen confederation that ruled eastern Anatolia, Iraq and Iran from Diyarbakır and later Tabriz. Ismail I’s Safavids replaced it in the early 1500s.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with the Kara Koyunlu, the Ottomans (Otlukbeli, 1473) and the Safavids.
profiles.story: Uzun Hasan exchanged envoys with Venice against the Ottomans.

profiles.name: Golden Horde
profiles.summary: The Golden Horde, or Ulus of Jochi, was the Mongol khanate of the western steppe, ruled from Sarai on the Volga. It took tribute from the Rus principalities. It split into separate khanates in the 1400s and its last remnant fell to the Crimean Khanate in 1502.
profiles.description: The Golden Horde, or Ulus of Jochi, was the Mongol khanate of the western steppe, ruled from Sarai on the Volga. It took tribute from the Rus principalities. It split into separate khanates in the 1400s and its last remnant fell to the Crimean Khanate in 1502.
profiles.conflicts: Kulikovo (1380); Timur’s campaigns (1390s); the Great Stand on the Ugra (1480).
profiles.story: Moscow stopped paying it tribute after 1480.

profiles.name: White Horde
profiles.summary: ‘White Horde’ is the name for the eastern wing of Jochi’s ulus, on the steppe of modern Kazakhstan. Historians use the term inconsistently. Its lands later became the base of the Uzbek and Kazakh khanates.
profiles.description: ‘White Horde’ is the name for the eastern wing of Jochi’s ulus, on the steppe of modern Kazakhstan. Historians use the term inconsistently. Its lands later became the base of the Uzbek and Kazakh khanates.
profiles.conflicts: Wars over the succession to the Golden Horde.
profiles.story: Tokhtamysh came from this wing before he took Sarai.

profiles.name: Khanate of Astrakhan
profiles.summary: Astrakhan was a Tatar successor of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga. Ivan IV annexed it in 1556, which gave Muscovy the whole Volga.
profiles.description: Astrakhan was a Tatar successor of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga. Ivan IV annexed it in 1556, which gave Muscovy the whole Volga.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with Crimea and the Nogais; Russian conquest (1556).
profiles.leaders: Its own line of Jochid khans.
profiles.story: Its fall opened the Caspian trade to Russia.

profiles.name: Khanate of Kazan
profiles.summary: Kazan was a Tatar khanate on the middle Volga, a successor of the Golden Horde. Ivan IV stormed Kazan in 1552.
profiles.description: Kazan was a Tatar khanate on the middle Volga, a successor of the Golden Horde. Ivan IV stormed Kazan in 1552.
profiles.conflicts: Repeated wars with Muscovy; siege of Kazan (1552).
profiles.story: St Basil’s Cathedral in Moscow celebrates Ivan IV’s capture of Kazan.

profiles.name: Nogai Horde
profiles.summary: The Nogai Horde was a confederation of Turkic nomads between the Volga and the Ural River, named after the Golden Horde general Nogai. Around 1600 it broke up under pressure from Russia and the Kalmyks.
profiles.description: The Nogai Horde was a confederation of Turkic nomads between the Volga and the Ural River, named after the Golden Horde general Nogai. Around 1600 it broke up under pressure from Russia and the Kalmyks.
profiles.conflicts: Raids on Muscovy; Kalmyk invasion (1630s).
profiles.culture: Nomadic horse breeders who supplied horses to Moscow.
profiles.story: Nogai horse herds were driven to Moscow to sell by the tens of thousands.

profiles.name: Kazakh Khanate
profiles.summary: The Kazakh Khanate was founded around 1465 by Janibek and Kerei. It ruled the steppe east of the Ural River and later split into three hordes, or juz. From the 1700s they gradually came under Russian rule.
profiles.description: The Kazakh Khanate was founded around 1465 by Janibek and Kerei. It ruled the steppe east of the Ural River and later split into three hordes, or juz. From the 1700s they gradually came under Russian rule.
profiles.conflicts: Wars with the Uzbeks and the Dzungars.
profiles.story: Kazakh historians date their statehood from 1465.

profiles.name: Finnmark
profiles.summary: Finnmark was Norway’s Arctic frontier, ruled for Denmark–Norway from the fortress of Vardøhus. Norwegian fishermen and Sámi lived there, and Sweden and Russia also claimed to tax the area.
profiles.description: Finnmark was Norway’s Arctic frontier, ruled for Denmark–Norway from the fortress of Vardøhus. Norwegian fishermen and Sámi lived there, and Sweden and Russia also claimed to tax the area.
profiles.conflicts: Kalmar War (1611–1613) over northern claims.
profiles.story: Vardø was the scene of witch trials in the 1600s.

profiles.name: Pontremoli
profiles.summary: Pontremoli is a town in the Lunigiana valley. Spanish Milan sold it to Genoa in 1647, and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany bought it in 1650. It stayed a Tuscan exclave until the 1840s.
profiles.description: Pontremoli is a town in the Lunigiana valley. Spanish Milan sold it to Genoa in 1647, and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany bought it in 1650. It stayed a Tuscan exclave until the 1840s.
profiles.conflicts: Its value as an Apennine pass was contested.
profiles.leaders: Medici and Lorraine grand dukes of Tuscany.
profiles.culture: A small market town on the Via Francigena.
profiles.story: Its castle, the Piagnaro, guards the pass.

profiles.name: Fivizzano
profiles.summary: Fivizzano was a Florentine, and later Tuscan, enclave in Lunigiana. It passed to Modena in the 1840s.
profiles.description: Fivizzano was a Florentine, and later Tuscan, enclave in Lunigiana. It passed to Modena in the 1840s.
profiles.conflicts: Border disputes among Tuscany, Modena and Genoa.
profiles.story: Jacopo da Fivizzano’s early printing press worked here in the 1470s.

profiles.name: Duchy of Modena and Reggio
profiles.summary: The Este family ruled Modena and Reggio. After losing Ferrara to the pope in 1598 they made Modena their capital. From 1814 a Habsburg-Este line ruled until 1859, when the duchy joined united Italy.
profiles.description: The Este family ruled Modena and Reggio. After losing Ferrara to the pope in 1598 they made Modena their capital. From 1814 a Habsburg-Este line ruled until 1859, when the duchy joined united Italy.
profiles.conflicts: Wars of the Spanish and Austrian Successions; the 1831 uprising; 1859.
profiles.culture: The Este court library and art collection.
profiles.story: The Biblioteca Estense keeps the Este Bible.

profiles.name: Duchy of Parma and Piacenza
profiles.summary: Parma and Piacenza were created as a duchy for the Farnese family in 1545. Spanish Bourbons followed in 1748. Napoleon’s widow Marie Louise ruled from 1814 to 1847. The duchy joined Italy in 1860.
profiles.description: Parma and Piacenza were created as a duchy for the Farnese family in 1545. Spanish Bourbons followed in 1748. Napoleon’s widow Marie Louise ruled from 1814 to 1847. The duchy joined Italy in 1860.
profiles.conflicts: Successions after the Farnese line ended in 1731.
profiles.culture: The Teatro Farnese and Correggio’s frescoes.
profiles.story: Marie Louise was a popular ruler in Parma.

profiles.name: Ritzebüttel (Cuxhaven)
profiles.summary: Ritzebüttel was Hamburg’s exclave at the mouth of the Elbe, including Cuxhaven. Hamburg held it from 1394 until 1937.
profiles.description: Ritzebüttel was Hamburg’s exclave at the mouth of the Elbe, including Cuxhaven. Hamburg held it from 1394 until 1937.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic occupation.
profiles.story: Cuxhaven was Hamburg’s outport.

profiles.name: Persia (Zand and Qajar)
profiles.summary: In 1789 Persia was moving from the Zand dynasty to the Qajars, who ruled until 1925. Russia took Persia’s Caucasus lands in the treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828). The Constitutional Revolution of 1906 created a parliament.
profiles.description: In 1789 Persia was moving from the Zand dynasty to the Qajars, who ruled until 1925. Russia took Persia’s Caucasus lands in the treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828). The Constitutional Revolution of 1906 created a parliament.
profiles.conflicts: Russo-Persian wars; the Anglo-Russian convention of 1907.
profiles.leaders: Agha Mohammad Khan; Fath-Ali Shah; Naser al-Din Shah.
profiles.story: Russia and Britain divided Persia into spheres of influence in 1907.

profiles.name: Khanates beyond Russia’s frontier
profiles.summary: The basemap uses this generic label in 1789 for the Muslim khanates on Russia’s southern frontier: the Kazakh hordes on the steppe and small khanates of the Caucasus and Central Asia (Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand). Russia conquered most of them in the 1800s.
profiles.description: The basemap uses this generic label in 1789 for the Muslim khanates on Russia’s southern frontier: the Kazakh hordes on the steppe and small khanates of the Caucasus and Central Asia (Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand). Russia conquered most of them in the 1800s.
profiles.conflicts: Russian expansion.
profiles.story: Russia annexed the Caucasus khanates first and the Central Asian ones later.

profiles.name: Bavarian Palatinate
profiles.summary: The Palatinate on the left bank of the Rhine. Austria and Bavaria jointly administered it in 1815, and it went to Bavaria in 1816.
profiles.description: The Palatinate on the left bank of the Rhine. Austria and Bavaria jointly administered it in 1815, and it went to Bavaria in 1816.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.story: The Hambach Festival of 1832 was a democratic rally held here.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Hohenzollern principalities
profiles.summary: The Swabian principalities of Hohenzollern-Hechingen and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. They passed to Prussia in 1850.
profiles.description: The Swabian principalities of Hohenzollern-Hechingen and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. They passed to Prussia in 1850.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.leaders: The Catholic Swabian branch of the Hohenzollerns.
profiles.story: Romania’s Carol I came from the Sigmaringen line.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz
profiles.summary: A small north German state that became a grand duchy in 1815.
profiles.description: A small north German state that became a grand duchy in 1815.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.story: Queen Louise of Prussia was born a princess of this house.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Grand Duchy of Hesse
profiles.summary: The Grand Duchy of Hesse, a grand duchy since 1806, gained Rhenish Hesse with Mainz in 1816 and received a constitution in 1820. It joined the German Empire in 1871.
profiles.description: The Grand Duchy of Hesse, a grand duchy since 1806, gained Rhenish Hesse with Mainz in 1816 and received a constitution in 1820. It joined the German Empire in 1871.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.leaders: Louis I, its first grand duke.
profiles.story: Under Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig, Darmstadt’s Mathildenhöhe artists’ colony (founded 1899) became a centre of Jugendstil.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Duchy of Nassau
profiles.summary: The Duchy of Nassau (1806–1866), ruled from Wiesbaden and the riverside palace of Biebrich. It backed Austria in 1866 and was annexed by Prussia.
profiles.description: The Duchy of Nassau (1806–1866), ruled from Wiesbaden and the riverside palace of Biebrich. It backed Austria in 1866 and was annexed by Prussia.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.story: Its last duke, Adolphe, became Grand Duke of Luxembourg in 1890, which is why Luxembourg’s ruling house is still Nassau.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Wetzlar
profiles.summary: Wetzlar was a former imperial city and the seat of the Imperial Chamber Court from 1689 to 1806. It became a Prussian exclave in 1815.
profiles.description: Wetzlar was a former imperial city and the seat of the Imperial Chamber Court from 1689 to 1806. It became a Prussian exclave in 1815.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.story: Goethe worked at the court here in 1772, which inspired The Sorrows of Young Werther.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Principality of Waldeck
profiles.summary: The Principality of Waldeck, ruled from Arolsen, was a tiny member of the German Confederation. From 1868 Prussia ran its administration by treaty while its princes kept the throne.
profiles.description: The Principality of Waldeck, ruled from Arolsen, was a tiny member of the German Confederation. From 1868 Prussia ran its administration by treaty while its princes kept the throne.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.story: Its princes served as commanders in many European armies.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

images.caption: Arolsen palace, seat of the princes of Waldeck
images.alt: Arolsen palace, seat of the princes of Waldeck

profiles.name: Principality of Lippe
profiles.summary: The Principality of Lippe, ruled from Detmold in the Teutoburg Forest, survived as a sovereign member of the German Confederation and the German Empire until 1918.
profiles.description: The Principality of Lippe, ruled from Detmold in the Teutoburg Forest, survived as a sovereign member of the German Confederation and the German Empire until 1918.
profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.story: The Hermannsdenkmal near Detmold, finished in 1875, honours Arminius’s victory over Rome in AD 9.

profiles.name: Duchy of Brunswick
profiles.summary: A Guelph duchy in Lower Saxony, restored in 1813 after six years inside Napoleon’s Kingdom of Westphalia. Its ‘Black Duke’ fell at Quatre Bras in 1815; a revolt in 1830 drove out his son Charles II and burned the Braunschweig palace. Brunswick joined the North German Confederation in 1867 and the German Empire in 1871.

profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.leaders: Frederick William, the ‘Black Duke’, killed at Quatre Bras (1815).
profiles.story: In 1809 Duke Frederick William led his black-uniformed ‘Black Brunswickers’ on a fighting march across Germany to the North Sea and escaped to England; they returned to fight in Spain and at Waterloo. Millais painted the legend in The Black Brunswicker (1860).
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Frederick William, duke of Brunswick”

profiles.name: Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin
profiles.summary: A Baltic grand duchy from 1815. It kept its old Estates constitution of 1755 and had no modern written constitution until 1918.

profiles.conflicts: Napoleonic wars; joined the German Confederation in 1815.
profiles.story: Schwerin Castle, rebuilt in 1845–57 on its island in the lake, became the showpiece of the grand dukes.

profiles.name: Thuringian states
profiles.summary: The basemap groups the small Thuringian states under one label. They included Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, which became a grand duchy in 1815, the Saxon duchies, Schwarzburg and Reuss. They were merged into the state of Thuringia in 1920.

profiles.name: Free City of Lübeck
profiles.summary: The former ‘Queen of the Hanse’, Lübeck was occupied by the French after the battle of Lübeck in 1806 and annexed to France in 1811. Restored as a free city in 1815, it kept its independence until Prussia absorbed it in 1937.
profiles.description: The former ‘Queen of the Hanse’, Lübeck was occupied by the French after the battle of Lübeck in 1806 and annexed to France in 1811. Restored as a free city in 1815, it kept its independence until Prussia absorbed it in 1937.
profiles.conflicts: French annexation (1810–1813).
profiles.story: Thomas Mann, born in Lübeck in 1875, drew on its merchant families for Buddenbrooks (1901). The Holstentor gate of 1478 still guards the old town.

profiles.name: Free City of Bremen
profiles.summary: A free Hanseatic city on the Weser that kept its sovereignty in the German Confederation in 1815. Because the river was silting up, Bremen bought land at the Weser mouth and founded Bremerhaven in 1827, which became one of Europe’s main emigrant ports to America.

profiles.conflicts: French annexation (1810–1813).
profiles.story: The stone Roland of 1404 in front of the town hall stood for the city’s liberties; the Rathaus and Roland are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2004).
sources: UNESCO World Heritage List, “Town Hall and Roland on the Marketplace of Bremen”

profiles.name: Free City of Hamburg
profiles.summary: Hamburg was a free Hanseatic city and became a sovereign member of the German Confederation in 1815. Annexed by France in 1810 and besieged under Marshal Davout in 1813–14, it rebuilt as Germany’s largest port. A great fire destroyed much of the old town in 1842, and the city joined the German customs union only in 1888.

Annexed by France in 1810 and besieged under Marshal Davout in 1813–14, it rebuilt as Germany’s largest port. profiles.conflicts: French annexation (1810–1813).
profiles.story: Hamburg is still a city-state of Germany today. Its neo-Renaissance Rathaus, finished in 1897, was built for a senate that still governs the city.

profiles.name: Grand Duchy of Oldenburg
profiles.summary: A North Sea duchy annexed by France in 1811 and restored in 1813; it was raised to a grand duchy in 1815. It joined the German Empire in 1871 and kept its grand dukes until 1918.

profiles.story: The ruling house was related to the Russian imperial family.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Electorate of Hesse (Hesse-Kassel)
profiles.summary: The Electorate of Hesse (Kurhessen), restored in 1813 under Elector William I. Its rulers kept the title of elector even after the Holy Roman Empire had gone. It sided with Austria in 1866 and was annexed by Prussia.

profiles.story: The Brothers Grimm worked in Kassel while collecting their fairy tales. Wilhelmshöhe palace later held the captured Napoleon III in 1870–71.
sources: T. Nipperdey, Germany from Napoleon to Bismarck (1996)

profiles.name: Duchy of Lucca
profiles.summary: A duchy created at the Congress of Vienna for Maria Luisa of Bourbon, the former queen of Etruria, as compensation until Parma passed to her line. Her son Charles Louis ruled from 1824; in 1847 he ceded Lucca to Tuscany and took Parma.

profiles.name: Free City of Kraków
profiles.summary: A free city under the joint protection of Austria, Prussia and Russia, created at the Congress of Vienna in 1815. With the Jagiellonian University and a small rural territory, it was the last independent fragment of Poland. Austria annexed it as the Grand Duchy of Kraków after the uprising of 1846.

profiles.name: Iceland
profiles.summary: Iceland in 1914 was under the Danish crown with home rule. The Althing was restored as an advisory body in 1845 and given legislative powers in 1874; home rule came in 1904 with Hannes Hafstein as minister. Iceland became a sovereign kingdom in personal union with Denmark in 1918 and a republic in 1944.
